pi.name: Patricia Wittkopp
pi.title: Deborah E. Goldberg Distinguished University Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and Arthur F. Thurnau Professor; Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Patricia (Trisha) Wittkopp earned a B.S. from the University of Michigan (1997) and a Ph.D. from the University of Wisconsin-Madison (2002), then was a Damon Runyon Fellow with Andy Clark at Cornell (2002-2005) before founding her lab at Michigan in August 2005. She served as EEB Department Chair (2020-2023), LSA Associate Dean for Natural Sciences (2023-2025), and is LSA Associate Dean for Research and Graduate Education (2025-present). Her honors include Guggenheim Fellow, AAAS Fellow, Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellow, a Humboldt Research Award, and the Margaret Dayhoff Mid-Career Award. Her lab studies the genetic basis of phenotypic evolution, with an emphasis on gene regulation in Drosophila and yeast.

description: The Wittkopp Lab investigates the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying phenotypic differences within and between species, with an emphasis on how transcriptional regulation converts genotype into phenotype. The lab integrates molecular and developmental biology, population and quantitative genetics, genomics, and bioinformatics, working primarily in Drosophila species and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Projects range from mechanistic studies of single cis-regulatory sequences and the yeast TDH3 promoter, to genome-wide quantification of cis- versus trans-regulatory contributions to expression variation, to characterizing the effects of new mutations and determining which become fixed within populations or between species. The lab is affiliated with EEB, MCDB, PIBS, the Center for Computational Medicine and Bioinformatics, and the Center for Statistical Genetics.

areas.title: Genetic mechanisms of phenotypic variation
areas.summary: The genetic and molecular basis of trait differences within and between species and their evolutionary origins, using comparative approaches across Drosophila species and yeast, including pigmentation and its role in behavior.

areas.title: Cis-regulatory sequence function and evolution
areas.summary: How non-coding DNA sequences control gene expression and how these regulatory regions change structurally over evolutionary time, through mechanistic single-gene studies.

areas.title: Cis- versus trans-regulatory contributions
areas.summary: Quantifying the relative contributions of cis- and trans-acting changes to genome-wide expression variation and how natural selection shapes their evolution, using population-level genomic approaches.

areas.title: Mutation properties and fixation
areas.summary: Characterizing the functional and fitness effects of newly arising mutations and determining which become established within populations or fixed between species, bridging molecular effects to population outcomes.

joining: Freshman and sophomore undergraduates can apply through the Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP) at the beginning of each year; juniors and seniors may pursue independent research for credit through their biology department. Prospective graduate students may apply through Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology, or the biomedical sciences (PIBS) programs and should contact Dr. Wittkopp directly during the application process. Postdoctoral openings depend on funding and lab size; interested candidates should email Dr. Wittkopp.
